analysis.one_liner: Creates a new federal commission to regulate major digital platforms on privacy, competition, and security.
analysis.headline: Sen. Warren's bipartisan bill to create a federal regulator for Big Tech was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new independent federal agency, the Digital Consumer Protection Commission, with sweeping power over large tech platforms: licensing dominant platforms, banning self-preferencing and conflicts of interest, restricting most new acquisitions, and enforcing a full privacy regime with duties of loyalty and care, limits on targeted advertising, and big penalties for data breaches. It would also ban noncompete agreements, no-poach agreements, and forced arbitration or class-action waivers by dominant platforms. The bill was introduced by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with Sen. Lindsey Graham as its only cosponsor, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday internet users gain enforceable privacy rights (access, correction, deletion, portability), protections against data breaches backed by damages and penalties of up to 15% of a parent company's annual revenue, and limits on targeted advertising. Workers at dominant platforms gain bans on noncompete, no-poach, and forced arbitration agreements. Small businesses that sell on major platforms gain rules against self-preferencing, tying, and platform conflicts of interest, plus data portability and interoperability.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users, platform workers, and small online sellers

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an independent, bipartisan 5-member commission to promote and enforce competition, privacy, transparency, and national security rules across all platform operators and covered entities.

Makes noncompete agreements, no-poach agreements, predispute arbitration agreements, and class-action waivers presumptively unlawful for dominant platforms, freeing their workers and business users to switch jobs or sue.

Requires operators of dominant platforms to obtain federal licenses, prohibits self-preferencing and platform conflicts of interest (with divestiture as the remedy), and bars dominant platforms from most acquisitions unless they prove by clear and convincing evidence the deal serves the public interest, with retrospective unwinding of past deals allowed.

Gives users duties-backed privacy rights (loyalty, care, mitigation, confidentiality), rights to access, correct, port, and delete their data, limits on targeted advertising, and civil penalties and damages for data breaches; penalties can reach 15% of the ultimate parent entity's total annual revenue, with personal liability for CEOs, CFOs, and security chiefs, and enforcement by states and private parties.
Requires dominant platforms to give users notice and an appeal when their content is restricted, and to publish their content-moderation criteria, with fines for violations.

analysis.who_pays: Large platform operators — companies clearing the bill's thresholds (roughly 50 million U.S. users and a $550 billion parent or 1 billion worldwide users) — would bear licensing, compliance, and divestiture costs, exposure to revenue-based penalties and personal executive liability, and a near-ban on acquisitions. Data brokers and the targeted-advertising economy would lose revenue from the privacy duties and advertising limits. Because the privacy duties apply to any company subject to the FTC Act, smaller websites and apps would also face new compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large tech platforms, data brokers, and adtech

drawbacks.text: The privacy duties apply to virtually every company subject to the FTC Act, not just Big Tech, so small websites, apps, and businesses would shoulder significant new compliance costs.

Requiring dominant platforms to prove that any acquisition serves the public interest, with possible unwinding of past deals, would cut off the acquisition route that many startups rely on as an exit and could slow venture investment in new companies.

Licensing dominant platforms, revocable by the commission, and mandated notice-and-appeal processes for content moderation would place a federal regulator inside platforms' moderation decisions, which critics across the spectrum warned could chill lawful speech and push platforms toward over-removal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-side benefits are substantial: a single regulator with real teeth on privacy, breaches, and platform self-dealing, plus worker protections like noncompete and arbitration bans. The costs are real too — a broad compliance burden on smaller companies, restrictions on startup exits through acquisition, and an unusually powerful new commission whose licensing and moderation-oversight powers raise free-speech and overreach concerns. On balance the bill was drafted to shift power from a handful of very large platforms to users, workers, and small sellers, and honest supporters would concede the design is aggressive and untested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, pairing with Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, who was the bill's only cosponsor.
That same day the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action of any kind appears in the record for the remaining 17 months of the 118th Congress: the committee never held a hearing or voted, and the full Senate never considered it.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large platform operators, data brokers, and the targeted-advertising economy are better off: no new regulator was created, so no licensing, divestiture, acquisition, or privacy regimes were imposed on them. The bill died without ever reaching a vote, so no senator had to take a position on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large platform operators and data brokers

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 27, 2023 and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan Warren-Graham introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote in the 17 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: As chair during the 118th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee action, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a single Republican cosponsor — a notable Warren-Graham pairing — but no committee or floor vote was ever held, so no party split ever appeared on the record.

industries.industry: Large platform operators (search, social media, e-commerce, app stores)
industries.note: The bill's thresholds target a handful of companies (roughly 50 million U.S. users with a $550 billion parent or 1 billion worldwide users) for licensing, divestiture of conflicting businesses, a near-ban on acquisitions, penalties up to 15% of parent revenue, and executive liability. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against the users, workers, and small sellers the bill was written to protect.

Data brokers are explicitly defined and covered, and the privacy duties restrict collecting, selling, and licensing personal data. Their revenue model of trading in personal information is what the bill's privacy title curtails.

The bill limits targeted advertising and restricts processing of sensitive personal data, cutting into the ad-targeting revenue that funds many platforms. Cheaper, less invasive advertising alternatives would not be restricted.

industries.industry: Small websites, apps, and online sellers
industries.note: They gain from rules against platform self-preferencing, tying, and forced arbitration, and from data portability, but because the privacy duties cover any company under FTC Act jurisdiction they also bear new compliance costs. Their interest mostly runs alongside users', with the compliance burden as the offset.
